rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all ten compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention window will guide subsequent narrowing and slope or temperature adjustments.
Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded central peaks respond to a shallower slope. This should improve separation while keeping the last peak near the ten-minute scoring threshold.

Raise the starting organic fraction and shorten the gradient while nearly preserving injection 2's successful slope. This removes low-organic time before the main peak cluster and should bring the last peak below ten minutes while retaining critical-pair resolution.
Slightly flatten injection 3's gradient to lift the remaining critical pair toward baseline resolution. The last peak should remain below ten minutes, potentially achieving the maximum CRF of 1.0.

Injection 4 already achieves the maximum CRF; increase temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature's effect on the critical pair.

Test whether a larger temperature shift carries the critical pair through its apparent selectivity crossover and restores separation in reversed order. Injection 4 remains the maximum-score reference while this run tests a faster high-temperature alternative.

Slightly flatten the high-temperature gradient to improve the newly limiting pair at R = 1.41. The last peak is expected to remain below ten minutes, allowing another maximum-score method if both critical pairs stay resolved.

Use a slope between injections 6 and 7 by lowering the endpoint to 0.90. This should retain full resolution while bringing the last peak out earlier than injection 7, with ample final organic strength for elution.

Shift injection 8's gradient window upward while preserving its slope to test whether the separation can finish sooner. Monitor both the early peaks and the critical central pairs, since a higher starting organic fraction can reduce their resolution.

Test a faster high-temperature regime where the limiting central pair may separate again after reversing elution order. Return phi0 to 0.15 to protect early-peak resolution, while retaining injection 8 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Test whether a steeper gradient improves the reversed central pair at 60 C, rather than flattening it back toward co-elution. This also probes a substantially faster separation; the maximum-score methods remain available if other pairs become limiting.

Explore the cooler selectivity regime, since warming initially compressed the critical pair at 40 C. A twelve-minute gradient tests whether cooling provides enough separation to shorten the method relative to injection 4 without creating another limiting pair.

Test the low-temperature endpoint to see whether the newly limiting pair separates after a selectivity crossover. Keeping injection 12's gradient unchanged isolates temperature effects, with the last peak expected to remain below ten minutes.

Lower the starting organic fraction to recover separation of the pair that worsened sharply in injection 9, while steepening the gradient to shorten elution. This tests whether improved initial retention permits a faster fully resolved method at 55 C.
Shorten injection 14's gradient by one grid step to seek an earlier last peak while preserving full resolution. This directly tests the speed limit of the promising lower-starting-organic method.

Choose a slope between injections 14 and 15 by reducing the endpoint to 0.85. This should restore the limiting pair above R = 1.5 while finishing slightly earlier than injection 14; the endpoint remains well above the observed elution window.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 16 to target a faster separation while keeping the limiting pairs above R = 1.5. The 0.75 endpoint remains comfortably above the last peak's estimated elution fraction of 0.56.

Test whether lowering the starting organic fraction further permits a steeper gradient without losing central-pair resolution. This could shorten elution relative to injection 17, though the other close pair may become limiting.

Slightly steepen injection 18's gradient to test the speed boundary of the fastest fully resolved method. Both central pairs have little resolution margin, so this run will establish whether further shortening is feasible at 55 C.

The 55 C speed boundary is now bracketed, with injection 18 retaining the maximum score. Test a steeper gradient at 50 C for an alternative elution-order regime that might resolve the central cluster in a substantially shorter run.

Refine the slope between injections 15 and 17 to test a slightly faster maximum-score method at phi0 = 0.10. The limiting pair is predicted to lie close to R = 1.5, while the other central pair should remain resolved.

Trim injection 18's gradient endpoint while preserving its successful slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. All peaks should still elute during the gradient, preserving maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a one-step temperature increase from injection 18 with its lower starting organic fraction, which has not yet been evaluated at 60 C. This isolates whether that window can retain full resolution while accelerating elution; injection 22 remains the compact maximum-score reference.

Return to 55 C and trim injection 16's endpoint while preserving its fully resolving slope. The last peak should still elute within the gradient, providing a compact maximum-score alternative with slightly more minimum-resolution margin than injection 22.

Use a slope between the fully resolved injections 7 and 8, with an endpoint above the last peak's elution window, to target maximum CRF with balanced critical-pair margins. Injection 22 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.
